speaker: narrator
text: He came from the Caribbean. A merchant's ledgers taught him to reckon; storms at sea taught him that a life could be rewritten overnight.

speaker: narrator
text: He put what he had seen into words. People read them and began to believe this young man deserved the chance to continue his education.

speaker: hamilton
text: I cannot take the island with me. But I can carry every word on the page. New York has schools, printing presses, and people willing to argue about the future. I will find my place there.

speaker: newsboy
text: News from the harbor! British troop movements, cargo prices, and a whole page of writers contradicting each other. Sir, do you want to know what is happening, or let people know who you are?

speaker: hamilton
text: Give me a copy first. Until I know what this city is arguing about, my writing will only be a conversation with myself.

speaker: citizen
text: More troops arrive every day. They say the army protects trade. But whose right to decide are they protecting?

speaker: loyalist
text: Without the Crown and its navy, what keeps order in this port? You would stake today's livelihood on a country that does not yet exist.

speaker: hamilton
text: Both are afraid of losing the lives they have. Neither has asked who has the right to make that wager for the other.

speaker: burr
text: You have been listening for a while. Alexander Hamilton, isn't it? I have read your work.

speaker: hamilton
text: Then we can skip the introductions. You heard them too: when they speak of freedom, they seem to mean entirely different things.

speaker: burr
text: Learn who is listening before you decide how much to say. Circumstances change. Words spoken in public remain.

speaker: hamilton
text: Observe first and understand where each side stands.

speaker: burr
text: Good. Patience can be a form of action. Come to the tavern. It is easier to hear people speak plainly there.

speaker: hamilton
text: And you? What do you believe?

speaker: burr
text: I believe in knowing people before making decisions. That question makes me more interested in knowing you. Come along.

speaker: hamilton
text: I support the revolution. You can put my name to it now.

speaker: burr
text: I heard you. So did the whole street. I hope you are ready to answer for a name spoken that loudly.

speaker: laurens
text: We write freedom in such large letters, yet always leave certain people outside the sentence. How will a country that still permits slavery explain its freedom?

speaker: hamilton
text: The answer you want may bring this table to a silence.

speaker: laurens
text: Then let it fall silent. What do you think matters most right now?

speaker: hamilton
text: Preserve order so people survive the war.

speaker: laurens
text: Surviving matters, of course. But some people have always been told to wait until later. We cannot keep saying that on their behalf.

speaker: hamilton
text: Who gets to decide, and who has the right to object?

speaker: laurens
text: Then remember to include those who have been excluded. Replacing the people in power is not enough.

speaker: hamilton
text: The promise of freedom must include enslaved people.

speaker: laurens
text: I would stand beside someone who believes that. But when that promise begins to trouble our allies, you must keep saying it.

speaker: laurens
text: You fall silent for a moment. That's all right. Listen to the others first; there will still be a place for you at this table.

speaker: lafayette
text: I did not cross the Atlantic to watch. But courage cannot fill a soldier's ration bag. Against a stronger army, where will you put your effort?

speaker: hamilton
text: Every path has a price. The difference is whether we are willing to choose for ourselves.

speaker: hamilton
text: Keep negotiating to give civilians room to breathe.

speaker: lafayette
text: Perhaps. But someone must stand guard outside the negotiating room. Do not mistake a breath of air for the end of the journey.

speaker: hamilton
text: Build alliances and turn an isolated struggle into a shared cause.

speaker: lafayette
text: Then you must learn to hear what your allies need. A shared cause cannot speak in only one person's voice.

speaker: hamilton
text: Demand independence openly, without waiting for permission.

speaker: lafayette
text: Direct enough. I like it. But after those words, the next step is preparing to march.

speaker: lafayette
text: You fall silent for a moment. That's all right. Listen to the others first; there will still be a place for you at this table.

speaker: mulligan
text: I've heard enough grand ideas. Tomorrow, ten people will help, a printer will extend credit, and there's an empty wagon. Hamilton, how will you use them?

speaker: hamilton
text: You have given me more than ten people. You have given me every street they know.

speaker: hamilton
text: Print a clear pamphlet to keep the conversation going in every street.

speaker: mulligan
text: Good. Fewer elegant phrases, more lines they can repeat to their neighbors.

speaker: hamilton
text: Deliver supplies first so people willing to join us can eat.

speaker: mulligan
text: I'll find the wagon. Be willing to do the work no one notices, and people will come to you again.

speaker: hamilton
text: Call a public meeting and make more people hear us today.

speaker: mulligan
text: We can find a place. But when the patrol arrives, you cannot think only of your speech.

speaker: mulligan
text: You fall silent for a moment. That's all right. Listen to the others first; there will still be a place for you at this table.

speaker: loyalist
text: Once you break from Britain, who escorts the ships, and who buys the cargo? You offer freedom as a guarantee, but ask every family to risk its livelihood.

speaker: citizen
text: That is what I want to know. Without tomorrow's bread, what good are today's slogans?

speaker: burr
text: They are waiting for your answer. Hear the whole question.

speaker: loyalist
text: After leaving Britain, who will escort the ships and buy the cargo? You ask each family to pay for freedom with tomorrow's bread.

speaker: hamilton
text: Count taxes and trade restrictions too.

speaker: hamilton
text: Those who pay should have a say.

speaker: hamilton
text: Why count only the costs of change?

speaker: hamilton
text: Let the dockworkers open their ledgers.

speaker: loyalist
text: Parliament has already considered every region. If each port insists on deciding for itself, what is left of the law?

speaker: hamilton
text: List the colonies' seats in Parliament.

speaker: hamilton
text: Those who obey laws should help make them.

speaker: hamilton
text: Considering us is not the same as hearing us.

speaker: hamilton
text: Who wants others to decide their taxes?

speaker: loyalist
text: The advocates of revolution only write essays. When food runs short, they will leave the poor to bear the consequences.

speaker: hamilton
text: Publish the supply plan and those responsible.

speaker: hamilton
text: Freedom cannot belong only to the well-fed.

speaker: hamilton
text: You have offered the poor no other path.

speaker: hamilton
text: Let workers and shopkeepers name their terms.

speaker: loyalist
text: The garrison is only here to keep order. If you have done nothing wrong, why fear more patrols?

speaker: hamilton
text: Examine the garrison's powers and costs.

speaker: hamilton
text: Power still needs the consent of the governed.

speaker: hamilton
text: Since when is asking for an explanation a confession?

speaker: hamilton
text: Let residents describe what patrols have changed.

speaker: loyalist
text: The empire has fleets and money. You do not even have a common supply ledger, yet you would lead everyone into war.

speaker: hamilton
text: Unify the ledgers and secure supplies item by item.

speaker: hamilton
text: Danger does not erase the right to choose.

speaker: hamilton
text: Your only plan is that we obey forever.

speaker: hamilton
text: Write down the work you are willing to do.

speaker: loyalist
text: Even if you win, who guarantees the new rulers will be better? You are exchanging one uncertainty for another.

speaker: hamilton
text: Put terms of office and accountability into law.

speaker: hamilton
text: Keep the people's right to replace their rulers.

speaker: hamilton
text: No guarantee does not mean no need for change.

speaker: hamilton
text: Tell us what you will no longer accept.

speaker: washington
text: I have read your essays. You make matters clear. But an army also needs people who finish the work.

speaker: hamilton
text: I want to lead troops. My ability should not stay on the page.

speaker: washington
text: Orders, intelligence, supplies. A wrong place name can cost lives. I need an aide. Are you willing to begin here?

speaker: washington
text: Your essays have reached camp. So has news of the argument in the street. You are good at drawing attention. Making yourself dependable is another matter.

speaker: hamilton
text: Then give me a company. I am willing to prove myself through action.

speaker: washington
text: Serve as my aide first. Orders, intelligence, and supplies also decide whether a company comes home. Will you take that responsibility?

speaker: hamilton
text: Accept the post and fulfill the responsibility at hand.

speaker: washington
text: Good. Several letters tonight cannot wait until tomorrow.

speaker: hamilton
text: Accept, while making clear that you want a future command.

speaker: washington
text: I have heard your request. Hear mine as well: prove through your present duties that I can trust you with the next ones.

speaker: hamilton
text: I belong on the battlefield and should be given command now.

speaker: washington
text: No one here receives command merely because he thinks he should. Tonight, you will still begin with these dispatches.

speaker: washington
text: The northern troops need supplies. Their camp, the departure time, and the destination are in these reports. Give the quartermaster an order he can carry out.

speaker: hamilton
text: One page. The reader must not have to guess, or search through fine prose to find his task.

speaker: hamilton
text: Deliver twenty barrels of flour and two crates of medicine.

speaker: hamilton
text: The receiving point is the northern riverside camp.

speaker: hamilton
text: Arrive before dawn tomorrow.

speaker: hamilton
text: The quartermaster leads a squad escorting the wagons.

speaker: hamilton
text: First, prevent the northern troops from running out of food.

speaker: hamilton
text: The old stone bridge is damaged; the eastern ferry still operates.

speaker: hamilton
text: The surgeon leads the stretcher party across the ferry.

speaker: hamilton
text: Move the seriously wounded to the rear hospital first.

speaker: hamilton
text: Bring bandages, water, and two empty wagons.

speaker: hamilton
text: Complete the transfer before sunset today.

speaker: hamilton
text: Finish preparations by six the morning after tomorrow.

speaker: hamilton
text: The first priority is to have every squad muster on time.

speaker: hamilton
text: The muster point is the clearing south of the mill.

speaker: hamilton
text: Each squad collects two days of rations and checks its ammunition.

speaker: hamilton
text: A messenger tells each squad leader to count their men.

speaker: narrator
text: In 1781, French and American forces surrounded Yorktown. Years of marches, dispatches, and disputes brought Hamilton to the foot of a British redoubt.

speaker: washington
text: You have this command. What I expect is an officer responsible for his whole company. Follow the plan. Do not turn it into a private test of your worth.

speaker: hamilton
text: I understand. After waiting so long, I cannot think only of how I will be seen.

speaker: narrator
text: In 1781, French and American forces surrounded Yorktown. Years of marches and dispatches brought Hamilton to the foot of a British redoubt.

speaker: washington
text: You have proved you can carry responsibility. These troops are yours. Follow the plan; when judgment is needed, I trust you to understand the purpose behind the order.

speaker: hamilton
text: This time, the names on the page will move forward beside me. I will remember that they need more than a fine sentence to follow.

speaker: hamilton
text: Confirm each squad's role and wait for the common signal.

speaker: hamilton
text: Every squad must know where the others are. When the signal comes, we move together.

speaker: hamilton
text: I will lead from the front. Stay close.

speaker: hamilton
text: I will step out first. But watch the signal. Do not lose your own position by following mine.

speaker: hamilton
text: Explain the shared objective so everyone knows why we are going.

speaker: hamilton
text: We are opening a breach in the siege. Remember the person beside you, and remember the way back. Now, take your positions.

speaker: hamilton
text: ADVANCE · Move forward

speaker: hamilton
text: HOLD · Steady the formation

speaker: hamilton
text: LEFT FLANK · Circle left

speaker: hamilton
text: ADVANCE · Move forward

speaker: hamilton
text: RIGHT FLANK · Support the right

speaker: hamilton
text: HOLD · Wait for allied troops

speaker: hamilton
text: LEFT FLANK · Support the flank

speaker: hamilton
text: ADVANCE · Cross the earthworks

speaker: hamilton
text: RIGHT FLANK · Maintain contact

speaker: hamilton
text: HOLD · Regroup

speaker: hamilton
text: ADVANCE · Enter the redoubt

speaker: hamilton
text: HOLD · Secure the position

speaker: narrator
text: Hamilton's troops took Redoubt No. 10, while French forces took the neighboring Redoubt No. 9. The siege tightened.

speaker: narrator
text: Days later, British forces surrendered at Yorktown. Victory belonged to many people fighting together. The war had not formally ended, but its course had changed.

speaker: hamilton
text: The hopes I once could only put in letters finally have weight. Tomorrow, someone will ask what we intend to do with this victory.
